readingInstruction: Read Ezekiel 25:1-28:26. This is a survey day. These are oracles against Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, and above all Tyre and its king. Look for the reasons given, and for one of the clearest echoes of the story of the fall of Satan.
settingTheScene: After the fall of Jerusalem is announced, Ezekiel turns to the nations around Judah. They had gloated over Jerusalem’s fall. The long oracle against Tyre in chapters 26 to 28 is the central part. Tyre was a wealthy commercial city on the Phoenician coast and the center of Mediterranean trade. Its king is addressed with language that goes beyond any human ruler.
observation: “Because you said, Aha! over my sanctuary when it was profaned… I will give you to the people of the East” (25:3-4).
“Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and will bring up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves” (26:3).
“You were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty” (28:12).
“You were in Eden, the garden of God” (28:13).
“You were an anointed guardian cherub. I placed you; you were on the holy mountain of God” (28:14).
“You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you” (28:15).
“Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor” (28:17).
“Thus says the Lord GOD: When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they are scattered… they shall dwell securely in it” (28:25-26).
interpretation:
The first oracles are brief. Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia are each condemned because they mocked or took vengeance on Judah. “Because you said Aha!” God takes personally what is done to his people. The vindication of his name is the repeated purpose: “Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

Tyre’s sin is arrogance. It rejoiced in Jerusalem’s downfall because it expected to profit from the loss of a trade rival. God promises the city’s destruction, with many nations coming against it like waves. Nebuchadnezzar besieged the mainland city for thirteen years, and Alexander the Great later destroyed the island fortress. Chapter 27 is a magnificent lament over Tyre as a great merchant ship laden with goods from all the world, which sinks.

Chapter 28 addresses the prince of Tyre first as a man who said, “I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods.” He is mocked: “You are indeed wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you.” Then, in verse 12, there is a lament for the “king of Tyre,” and the language soars beyond any human king. He was in Eden. He was an anointed guardian cherub on the holy mountain of God. He was blameless until iniquity was found in him. He was cast out in pride. Many readers, from early church writers on, see in this an echo of the fall of Satan, the power behind pride. Whether or not the language refers directly to him, the pattern is the same as in Isaiah 14: pride goes before a fall.

The chapter ends with a promise to Israel. God will gather his people, and they will dwell in security, with no more pricking briers or painful thorns among their neighbors. The enemies who mocked will be removed, and God’s holiness will be shown.
connection: Luke 10:18: Jesus said, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.” 1 Timothy 3:6 warns that a recent convert may fall into the condemnation of the devil through conceit. Revelation 18 laments the fall of Babylon in terms like Ezekiel 27. Proverbs 16:18: “Pride goes before destruction.” James 4:6: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” Philippians 2:5-8 shows Christ, who humbled himself, the opposite of the king of Tyre.
application:
Examine where pride or self-sufficiency has crept in. Humble yourself before God.

Do not rejoice when others fall. Ask God to guard your heart from the spirit of “Aha!”

Look to Jesus, who did not count equality with God something to be grasped, but humbled himself.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to guard you from pride in gifts and wealth.
Ask him to keep you from rejoicing in another’s downfall.
Thank him for giving grace to the humble.
